## 2. Three distinct screens

### G: equivariant hypersymplectic deformation

The screened target is: for a finite smooth group action on a closed connected oriented four-manifold X preserving each member of a normalized positive closed triple, construct a group-invariant positive triple path, in the three original classes, to a hyperkahler triple. This is a fixed action, including possible fixed points; abstract existence of some action on a diffeomorphic K3 or torus is insufficient.

HY already gives the one-point, fixed-class deformation, the separate Kahler realization of each nonzero constituent, and the standard K3/T4 smooth types. It also has a genuine smooth family operation: `05-families.tex`, `lem:compatible-family`, constructs closed compatible forms over the coefficient sphere using a rank-two kernel bundle and a smooth elliptic right inverse. `09-regular-preparation.tex`, `lem:smooth-tamers`, chooses tamers along a supplied family, with endpoints fixed. These are not missing achievements to nominate. Conversely they do not select the whole fibration, primitive null class, nodal preparation and auxiliary solution equivariantly.

The free-action subclass is technical and closed: descend the forms to Y=X/G, multiply by sqrt(|G|) to normalize their intersection matrix on Y, use HY there, divide by sqrt(|G|), and lift. The lifted path is G-invariant and has the original classes. Every operation is on a closed smooth manifold because the action is free. In the presence of fixed points the quotient is not supplied as a smooth manifold, and an orbifold/resolution/relative-divisor theorem cannot be substituted for HY. Averaging third-form tamers for an already invariant J works by convexity; averaging arbitrary positive triples does not. Pointwise, the triples (A,C,B) and (A,-C,-B) can each have Gram matrix I while their average has rank one. This is an obstruction to that averaging rule, not a same-class global counterexample to G.

HY's endpoint chooses an integral null class, changes the coefficient basis, constructs and prepares a nodal fibration, then fixes one small auxiliary parameter before two Kahler steps. The constant-rank correction does not choose those discrete/geometric data around a parameter loop. Nor does pointwise transversality automatically survive restriction to invariant perturbations at fixed points. Thus G remains open here. No family theorem, simultaneous Moser transport or higher-dimensional ball-complement consequence is claimed.

## 3. Exact pressure identities

The analytic arguments in this section are proved here, including the standard harmonic-moment criterion. No priority is claimed for that criterion or for higher-moment pressure obstructions. Write `G(x)=1/(4 pi |x|)`, so `-Delta G=delta_0`. For a smooth compactly supported divergence-free velocity v define

`S_v=partial_i partial_j(v_i v_j)`, `p_v=G*S_v`.

Then `-Delta p_v=S_v` and p_v is the decaying pressure compatible with a solenoidal force. Smoothness follows, for instance, by moving any number of derivatives to the smooth compact source before convolution with the locally integrable G. Outside the velocity support p_v is harmonic. If v and p_v are compactly supported then `v_t+(v.grad)v+grad p_v-nu Delta v` is compactly supported and divergence free; the pressure sign here matches `u_t+(u.grad)u=-grad p+nu Delta u+f`.

**Lemma 3.1 (moment criterion).** If `supp v` is contained in a ball B_R, then p_v vanishes outside that ball if and only if

`M_v(H):=integral v_i v_j partial_ij H =0`

for every harmonic polynomial H. Degrees zero and one vanish automatically. Necessity follows by two integrations by parts and `Delta H=0`. For sufficiency, expand `G(x-y)` in solid harmonics in y for |y|<|x|. On each exterior set |x|>=R+epsilon the series and its required derivatives converge uniformly on the support, so its pairing with S_v is the sum of zero moments. This gives p_v=0 for |x|>R; no boundary limit is interchanged with a nonuniform series. The necessity identity also shows that degree-two cancellation is exactly `integral v_i v_j=c delta_ij`. This familiar isotropy condition is necessary, not sufficient in general.

**Lemma 3.2 (one radial swirl).** Let a be a unit vector, c a center, and f a smooth radial profile supported in a compact subinterval of (0,infinity). Put `w(c+y)=f(|y|)(a cross y)` and `I_f=integral_0^infinity f(r)^2 r^4 dr`. Then w is divergence free and for every harmonic polynomial H,

`M_w(H)=-(4 pi/3) I_f (a.grad)^2 H(c)`.                 (3.1)

In particular, outside the swirl's outer radius,

`p_w(c+y)=-(I_f/3)|y|^(-3)[3(a.y/|y|)^2-1]`.          (3.2)

Proof: the vector field a cross y is tangent to spheres and divergence free, hence annihilates f. Set `L=(a cross y).grad` and `F=f^2`. Since integration of L against radial volume is zero,

`integral F w0_i w0_j H_ij = integral F[L^2 H-(a cross(a cross y)).grad H]`

`= integral F[ y.grad H-(a.y)(a.grad H)]`,

where w0=a cross y and |a|=1. The first integral is zero by the mean-value property of the harmonic H. If h is harmonic, its first spherical moment is `integral_{S2} omega_i h(c+r omega) d omega=(4 pi r/3) partial_i h(c)`: expand in harmonic homogeneous polynomials, or differentiate the mean-value formula on balls and use the divergence theorem. Apply this with h=(a.grad)H. Radial integration proves (3.1). The exterior expansion in Lemma 3.1 identifies p_w with `-(4 pi/3)I_f partial_aa G(y)`, proving (3.2). This proves cancellation of all degrees, not only a far-field asymptotic.

For direct evaluation one can avoid a three-dimensional singular integral. In polar coordinates with axis a, the source is `S_0(r)+S_2(r) P_2(a.y/r)`, where

`S_0=-2F-(2/3)r F'`, `S_2=(2/3)r F'`, `P_2(z)=(3z^2-1)/2`.

For l=0,2 set

`Q_l(r)=1/(2l+1)[r^(-l-1) integral_0^r s^(l+2)S_l(s)ds + r^l integral_r^infinity s^(1-l)S_l(s)ds]`. (3.3)

Then `p_w=Q_0(r)+Q_2(r) P_2(a.y/r)`, where Q_l are radial coefficients and P_2 is the Legendre polynomial. These formulas solve `-Delta p=S_w` and decay at infinity. Near r=0 they are a constant plus a harmonic quadratic polynomial because f vanishes on an inner ball. Thus no singular evaluation at r=0 is needed. They also give computable smoothness and every derivative bound from one-dimensional integrals of fixed smooth profiles. Outside the support the l=0 coefficient is zero and the l=2 coefficient is `-(2/3) I_f r^(-3)`, agreeing with (3.2).

**Lemma 3.3 (pressure-balanced rotation gate).** Choose three smooth radial profiles f_0,f_1,f_2 with disjoint closed supports and with the same positive I_f. Choose orthonormal axes a_0,a_1,a_2. Then

`V(y)=sum_{j=0}^2 f_j(|y|)(a_j cross y)`

has compact pressure P supported inside the largest outer radius. Indeed the disjoint radial supports eliminate all cross products in V tensor V. Equation (3.2) gives an exterior pressure proportional to `sum_j[3(a_j.omega)^2-1]=0`. P is the sum of the three smooth Newtonian pressures, so it is smooth across the outer sphere as well. In any annulus where f_0=1 and f_1=f_2=0, V is exactly the rigid rotation generator a_0 cross y. Its trajectories stay on spheres about zero, hence never reach the two auxiliary annuli.

Such profiles are effective: choose any nonzero nonnegative smooth bumps for the two auxiliary annuli and a plateau bump for the active annulus, using RV's computably smooth cutoff. Multiply each auxiliary bump by `sqrt(I_0/I_j)`. Each denominator has an effective strictly positive lower bound by integration on a rational subinterval where that bump is bounded below. No noncomputable square root or exact-zero test is involved. The auxiliary factors may be large but are fixed constants independent of the machine, step and grid address.

The velocity V is **not** asserted to be a stationary Euler solution. Its acceleration plus grad P is a generally nonzero compact solenoidal field. This distinction is essential: no Gavrilov localizability hypothesis is being assumed for the elementary radial swirls.

## 4. Constructive route A: preserve an arbitrary core field

The first route tries to leave an arbitrary core velocity exactly unchanged and cancel its pressure by remote fields. It establishes finite moment completion but is not used to claim a general all-order extension theorem.

**Lemma 4.1 (finite completion, all finite degrees paid).** Let v be an effectively smooth divergence-free field supported in B_r, and fix a finite N>=2 and radii r<rho<R. There is a finite sum w of disjoint radial swirl fields, supported in B_R outside B_r, such that v+w is divergence free, equals v on B_r, and `M_{v+w}(H)=0` for every harmonic polynomial of degree at most N. The construction is effective for supplied smooth data and effective support/derivative bounds.

Proof: take a real orthonormal basis Y_lm of spherical harmonics for normalized sphere measure and write `H_lm(x)=|x|^l Y_lm(x/|x|)`. Put

`b(omega)=B+sum_{l=2}^N sum_m M_v(H_lm)/[l(l-1)rho^(l-2)] Y_lm(omega)`,

where B is any computable strict upper bound for the absolute value of the nonconstant sum. Choose a positive finite cubature on S2 exact for polynomials through degree 2N. One explicit construction uses N+1 Gauss-Legendre nodes in z and 2N+1 equally spaced azimuths. The azimuth sum kills every nonzero mode with |m|<=2N; the zero mode is a polynomial in z of degree <=2N, integrated exactly by Gauss quadrature. Its nodes, positive weights and a positive minimum separation are effective algebraic/trigonometric data. For completeness, the degree-(N+1) Legendre polynomial has N+1 simple roots in (-1,1): otherwise the polynomial formed from its sign-changing roots in that interval has smaller degree and has a nonzero, constant-sign product integral with it, contradicting orthogonality. Polynomial division then proves exactness through degree 2N+1. Applying exactness to the square of each cardinal polynomial proves strict positivity of the corresponding weight. The roots and weights are computable. A harmonic basis can likewise be constructed by a finite rational Laplacian kernel computation followed by Gram-Schmidt for sphere moments; a strict B is obtained from coefficient bounds and rational upper enclosures for the finitely many moments.

For each node omega_j put a swirl of axis omega_j at c_j=rho omega_j in a small disjoint ball inside the allowed annulus, with `(4 pi/3)I_j=w_j b(omega_j)`. Its amplitude is computable from this positive number. Euler's identity gives `partial_{omega_j omega_j}H_lm(rho omega_j)=l(l-1)rho^(l-2)Y_lm(omega_j)`. Equation (3.1), cubature and orthogonality show that the added moment is exactly -M_v(H_lm). Different supports eliminate cross terms. This proves the finite claim.

The construction uses all possible harmonic coefficients of the supplied core field, not a computation trace. Applied to a finite RV time slot these coefficients are finite integrals of its all-address formula. There is no requirement to know which code the observed particle reaches.

**Why this route was not used as a completed infinite theorem.** Making N large gives increasingly many, increasingly small swirl supports and no uniform C-infinity bound from Lemma 4.1 alone. A possible infinite shell scheme places degree cutoffs N_j on radii rho_j increasing to R and estimates the next tail using `(rho_{j-1}/rho_j)^l`. Polynomially shrinking shell gaps and rapidly increasing N_j could beat derivative costs. But this needs a quantitative cubature separation bound, all time derivatives of the coefficient correction, positive square-root margins, and a computable common tail modulus at the limiting sphere. None follows by taking an unqualified diagonal limit of Lemma 4.1. The finite theorem is proved; the arbitrary-core, smooth all-time infinite completion is an **open extension within this report**, and C80 does not depend on it.

## 7. Stress tests and limits of the proof

The diagnostic program checks exact rational identities, not asymptotic or universal truth. The universal arguments are the written proofs above.

- Harmonic-moment tests span the full rational kernel of the Laplacian in each tested degree, rather than checking only one zonal harmonic. They check translated radial swirls and the coefficient of each independent radial moment. Only the second derivative at the center survives.
- The exterior-pressure cancellation is pointwise in direction and follows from three orthogonal axes at one center with equal I. Different centers, unequal I, or overlapping radial supports destroy that proof. The six-center fourth-harmonic example is retained as an adversarial test.
- Two half-turns at scale delta_n would move a distance of order delta_n and would not obey the all-order small-velocity budgets. A half-turn at scale b_n would cost inverse powers of b_n. The small-angle inverse formula is essential.
- The exact matrix test checks the order and sign in (5.2). Interchanging c_1 and c_2 or omitting the J term fails the translation identity.
- Radius bounds include the first-pulse displacement before the second pulse, both auxiliary annuli, and all support centers. Address disjointness is checked for the pressure as well as velocity. It is insufficient to check only center endpoints.
- Nonhalting x_1 is fixed at every intermediate time because only the primary swirl acts on that path and its axis is e_1. Auxiliary axes need not preserve x_1 elsewhere. The theorem concerns one fixed marked particle.
- Loading is separately constructed with x_1>=-1. No assumption about an unexamined loading segment is made.
- Nonzero pressure and nonlinear compact force are essential. This is not an unforced or zero-pressure Euclidean universality result. Compact stationary Euler examples cannot be substituted without checking their actual gate maps.
- The signal at a halt in slot n is b_n, tending to zero. No positive global measurement margin follows. Late force evaluation can be extremely expensive; the theorem is computable, not an efficiency result.

## 8. Contribution comparison and status

The mathematical change is the intersection of exact locality of the velocity/pressure/force and solenoidality of the force, under the RV time/derivative budgets. The compiler, the unit physical clock, finite total particle length, exact shrinking detector, viscosity scope, residual realization, and halting equivalence are attributed to source operations. The new work must stand or fall on the pressure-balanced gate and its small-angle implementation, not on an ordinary undecidability reduction.

The strongest source operations do not suffice by an unchanged application: the Euclidean RV/IB/SP residual generally has nonzero divergence; its periodic Leray projection is on a compact torus; Euclidean projection introduces a nonlocal pressure gradient. GS/FS transverse shears have vanishing convection and direct solenoidal forcing in their torus setting, but a nonzero field independent of its direction of travel cannot have compact support in that direction in R3. Localizing it destroys that unchanged property. A general compactly supported volume-preserving isotopy does not make its pressure compact. Section 3 pays exactly this nonlinear compatibility.

Primary comparison is deliberately bounded. Cardona–Miranda–Peralta-Salas, arXiv:2111.03559v3, gives fixed-Euclidean Beltrami computation with noncompact computational geometry and infinite energy; its torus result and viscous remark concern tape-bounded computation and nonzero Beltrami initial velocity. Dyhr–Gonzalez-Prieto–Miranda–Peralta-Salas, arXiv:2507.07696v1 and the UPC-hosted April 15, 2026 manuscript (watermarked DRAFT; the publisher page was inaccessible), obtain stationary unforced computation after deforming a Hodge-admissible metric; harmonic initial velocity is nonzero. These do not supply C80's zero-data fixed-Euclidean compact control.

Gavrilov's compact stationary Euler flow and Constantin–La–Vicol's localizable Grad–Shafranov construction are important precedents for nonlinear compact pressure. Their constraint `u.grad p=0` and stationary Euler balance are different from Lemma 3.3, which permits a nonzero compact solenoidal acceleration and realizes prescribed rigid rotations on a plateau. No statement that compact pressure itself is new is made. [Brandolese–Meyer](https://www.numdam.org/item/10.1051/cocv:2002021.pdf), Remark 2.6 and Corollary 2.7, also give higher-moment polynomial-divisibility obstructions; Theorem 3.1 and Section 4 relate their persistence and discrete symmetries to improved algebraic spatial decay. Both quadratic isotropy and the general hierarchy of moment obstructions are prior ideas. The finite-mode control theorem of [Brandolese–Okabe](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.12733) uses a matrix divergence-form force and small initial data; its rapid dissipation is the stated little-oh energy rate, not compact velocity and pressure with all-order temporal decay. The proposed contribution here is the explicit finite all-moment cancellation compatible with an active rotation plateau, followed by the small-angle gate estimate. The fourth-harmonic test explains why imposing only quadratic isotropy or cubic symmetry would leave a real gap.
